claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments in a copper matrix.
A thin thermal-barrier interlayer can be deposited between the tungsten and copper phases.
The interlayer will suppress phase separation at the W–Cu interface.
The interlayer will suppress interfacial void formation.
The interlayer will improve thermal conductivity under combined heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relative to an untreated composite.
The interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier.
Acting as a diffusion barrier reduces interfacial reactions between tungsten and copper.
The interlayer limits atomic intermixing at the W–Cu interface.
Atomic intermixing at the W–Cu interface leads to phase separation.
The interlayer inhibits nucleation and growth of interfacial voids during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Maintaining interfacial integrity reduces thermal resistance caused by voids and phase-separated regions.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance produces higher thermal conductivity than in the untreated composite.
An untreated W–Cu composite develops phase separation and interfacial voids under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The hypothesis is intended to apply under moderate thermal cycling and irradiation typical of plasma-facing-material and cooling-channel joints.
The intervention may cease to work at temperatures above 1000°C.
The intervention may cease to work at irradiation doses far above conventional service levels.
